intro: Cambridge's remarkable trees split between college gardens and the University Botanic Garden. The colleges hold a mulberry that grew back from its own roots after a 1795 storm, an apple grafted in 1954 from the tree behind Newton's theory of gravity, and a plane raised from seed carried home from Thermopylae. The Botanic Garden adds a redwood from the first seed shipped out of California, a one-off hybrid oak, black pines Darwin's teacher planted to look mismatched, a wingnut thicket born of an 1886 storm, a 1949 dawn redwood and a champion nut pine that survived a 2000 storm.
meta_description: Cambridge's remarkable trees: the Milton Mulberry, Trinity's Newton apple graft, Henslow's black pines and the Botanic Garden's 1949 dawn redwood.
question_answer: Cambridge's oldest tree by documented lineage is the Milton Mulberry at Christ's College, grown from the root of a tree planted in 1608 or 1609, the year after John Milton's birth, and still fruiting today despite being uprooted by a storm in 1795. It stands in the Fellows' Garden, viewable as part of a visit to Christ's College in the city centre.
question_meta: The Milton Mulberry at Christ's College, regrown from a tree planted in 1608-1609, is Cambridge's oldest tree by documented lineage, still fruiting today.
question_context: Christ's College planted a mulberry tree in 1608 or 1609, the year after the poet John Milton was born, as part of King James I's push to build an English silk industry by planting mulberries nationwide for silkworms to feed on. Milton studied at Christ's from 1625 to 1629, by which point the tree was already tall, and tradition holds he spent time beneath it, though no record proves he did. The silk scheme failed everywhere, since the species James's advisors chose feeds silkworms poorly, but the mulberry itself survived over a century after the industry died. In 1795 a storm uprooted the tree entirely. Rather than replace it, the college's gardeners let it regrow from its own root, propped on wooden posts ever since, and it still produces a real crop of mulberries each summer, harvested by the college's own gardeners and turned into jam for the kitchens. What stands in the Fellows' Garden today is not, strictly, the tree Milton studied under, but it grew from the same root, in the same spot, without a single year's gap.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cambridge?
faq.a: The Milton Mulberry at Christ's College, grown from the root of a tree planted in 1608 or 1609. A 1795 storm uprooted the original, but it regrew from the same root rather than being replaced, and still fruits today.

faq.q: Is Newton's apple tree in Cambridge real?
faq.a: The Trinity College tree, planted in 1954, is a genuine graft from the actual apple tree at Newton's childhood home, Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, reputed to be the tree that inspired his theory of gravity. It is not the original tree, but it is a direct vegetative descendant of it.

faq.q: Where did the plane tree at Jesus College come from?
faq.a: A seed collected in 1802 at Thermopylae, Greece, the site of the ancient battle, by Jesus College fellow Edward Daniel Clarke during his travels. It was planted in the college's Fellows' Garden and now stands over 25 metres tall.

faq.q: Is Cambridge University Botanic Garden free to visit?
faq.a: No, the Botanic Garden charges admission, with free entry for University of Cambridge students, staff and card-carrying members. It is open daily except Christmas Day and Boxing Day.

trees.name: Newton's Apple Tree

location.address: Outside the main gate, Trinity College, Trinity Street, Cambridge CB2 1TQ

trees.story:
This is not Newton's apple tree, and it is genetically the same tree. The one he described stood at his family home, Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, and the falling-apple story comes from accounts he gave late in life rather than from anything in Cambridge. That original died around 1815 to 1820. Before it did, cuttings and grafts were taken and propagated onward as a genetically identical line, and in 1954 Trinity College planted one of them outside its main gate, directly below the room Newton lived in as a student.

So the tree in front of you is 72 years old and its tissue traces back, graft by graft, to the actual tree behind one of science's most famous stories. That is the whole reason to stop.

It is a 'Flower of Kent', an old English cooking variety, which means the fruit is edible and unremarkable: tart, disease-prone, nobody's choice for flavour. Newton would have known it as a kitchen apple rather than anything special.

It stands fenced for protection on Trinity Street, visible from the pavement outside the gate at any hour, and it is a five-minute walk from the older tree on this list, the Milton Mulberry at Christ's College, which was already grown when Newton arrived.
trees.access: Free, visible from Trinity Street outside the college gate at any time
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Cambridge railway station
trees.notes: Distinguished carefully in research from a separate, similarly-named tree: Cambridge University Botanic Garden had its own Woolsthorpe-grafted 'Newton's Apple Tree' on Brookside lawn, which was blown down by Storm Eunice in February 2022 and has not been replaced with a mature specimen (young grafted clones are still in the garden's nursery). This entry is the Trinity College specimen, a separate tree at a separate site, planted 1954, confirmed alive and visitor-accessible as recently as June 2025 per multiple visitor reports checked this run. Age calculated from the 1954 planting date to 2026. Woolsthorpe Manor itself (Newton's family home, where the original tree stood) is in Lincolnshire, well outside Cambridge, and is not this entry's subject. Photo: Wikimedia Commons file '"Newton's" apple tree, Trinity College - geograph.org.uk - 5599349.jpg' (N Chadwick, CC BY-SA 2.0), part of the dedicated Commons category for this specific tree, no identity ambiguity.

best_time.label: September, when the historic 'Flower of Kent' apples ripen

trees.name: The Milton Mulberry

location.address: Fellows' Garden, Christ's College, Saint Andrew's Street, Cambridge CB2 3BU

trees.story: James I wanted England to have a silk industry to rival France and Italy, and in the early 1600s ordered mulberry trees planted nationwide to feed silkworms. Christ's College planted one in its Fellows' Garden in 1608 or 1609, the year after the poet John Milton was born; by the time Milton arrived as a student in 1625, the tree was already established, and college tradition holds he spent time beneath it, though no contemporary record proves it directly. The silk scheme collapsed everywhere in England, partly because James's advisors specified the wrong species for silkworms to thrive on, but the mulberry outlived the industry it was planted for by well over a century. In 1795 a storm uprooted it completely. Rather than replace it with a sapling, the college's gardeners let it regrow from its own root system, and what stands today, propped on wooden posts, low and sprawling with trunks and branches poking out at odd angles from a raised mound, has been growing continuously from that same root for well over two centuries since. It still produces a real crop of mulberries each summer, which the college's gardeners harvest and turn into jam for the kitchens.
trees.access: Christ's College Fellows' Garden, limited public visiting hours (check college website)
trees.transport: 12 min walk from Cambridge railway station
trees.notes: Corroborated by Christ's College's own official page (which itself notes the 1608 vs 1609 discrepancy between popular retellings and the college archives, resolved here in favour of the college's own archival figure, 1609) and Morus Londinium, a dedicated mulberry-tracking research project. Age range spans both the technically-accurate 'grown from the same root since 1795' figure (231 years) and the popularly-cited 'planted 1609' figure (417 years) that the college itself uses in visitor-facing material, since the tree is honestly a continuous regrowth of the original root rather than either a new planting or literally the same trunk Milton saw. Presented in the story as a living continuation, the same honest framing precedent used for Paris's Elm of Saint-Gervais. Photo: Wikimedia Commons file 'Milton's Mulberry Tree - geograph.org.uk - 8115998.jpg' (Mr Ignavy, CC BY-SA 2.0, photographed 17 April 2025), filed in the Fellows' Garden category and tagged 'Morus nigra', a recent, clearly identified photo of this exact tree. Viewed directly 2026-07-31: shows a wider Fellows' Garden view with several bare-season trees, a church spire and a greenhouse visible; one low, spreading, gnarled tree near the centre is plausibly the propped mulberry by its habit, but no supporting post or plaque is visible to confirm it against the other trees in frame with certainty. Kept at found_needs_check rather than approved, since the filename/category is a strong identity signal but this session couldn't visually confirm which specific tree in the frame it names, per the Cadiz standard's own rule against approving from a filename or description alone.

best_time.label: August into September, when the mulberries ripen

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Jesus College

location.address: Fellows' Garden, Jesus College, Jesus Lane, Cambridge CB5 8BL

trees.story: Edward Daniel Clarke, a Jesus College fellow and later Cambridge's first professor of mineralogy, spent the years around 1800 travelling through Greece, Egypt and the Ottoman Empire, a journey that eventually filled six published volumes and made him one of the era's best-known explorer-scholars. In 1802, at Thermopylae, the narrow pass where three hundred Spartans and their allies held off the Persian army in 480 BC, Clarke collected seed from the plane trees growing there. He brought it home to Jesus College and had it raised into seedlings; one of them was planted in the Fellows' Garden the same year. Oriental Planes are long-lived, broad-crowned trees native across the eastern Mediterranean, and this one has had well over two centuries in an English college garden to put on size, now standing more than 25 metres tall. It is a genuinely unusual case among Cambridge's collected trees: not a symbolic gift or a scientific graft, but a seed one traveller happened to pick up at one of the most storied battle sites in Western history and carry home in his luggage.
trees.access: Jesus College Fellows' Garden, limited public visiting hours (check college website)
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Cambridge railway station
trees.notes: Corroborated by Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society's reference site, independent horticultural authority) and Capturing Cambridge (a local history archive project), both giving the same account: seed collected by Edward Daniel Clarke at Thermopylae in 1802, planted the same year in the Fellows' Garden. Height (over 25m) and the '11 seedlings raised, this one planted' detail from the same two sources. Age calculated from 1802 planting to 2026.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big plane in the Fellows' Garden, over 25 metres tall, grown from seed collected at Thermopylae and planted here in 1802.

trees.name: The Giant Redwood of the Botanic Garden

location.address: Main Walk, Cambridge University Botanic Garden, Cambridge CB2 1JE

trees.story: In 1852, the Cornish plant collector William Lobb reached Calaveras Grove in California and became one of the first Europeans to see Giant Redwoods growing wild, trees already thousands of years old and taller than anything in Britain. Recognising what he had found, he cut his expedition short and raced seed back to England for the Veitch nursery in Exeter, which was selling seedlings within a year, an unusually fast turnaround for a tree nobody in Europe had grown before. Cambridge University Botanic Garden was among the very first customers, planting out its own seedlings around 1855. Two of that original planting still stand on opposite sides of the garden's Main Walk near the fountain, and a third, at the junction with Henslow Walk, has grown into the tallest tree in the entire garden at just over 30 metres. Redwoods take centuries to reach the scale they are famous for in California, so at under two hundred years old this specimen is, by the standards of its own species, still young, a fast-growing adolescent rather than anything close to the giants Lobb originally found.

trees.name: The Cambridge Oak

location.address: Near the Terrace Garden, Cambridge University Botanic Garden, Cambridge CB2 1JE

trees.story: Most oaks on this site are one of a small handful of well-known species. The Cambridge Oak is not: it is a hybrid, most likely a cross between the evergreen Quercus rugosa, native to Mexico and the southwestern United States, and Britain's own native Pedunculate Oak, a pairing that should not naturally occur an ocean apart and that appears to exist, in this precise combination, only here. It came from the Worcester nursery of Messrs Smith sometime between 1873 and 1875 and was planted in Cambridge University Botanic Garden soon after. By 1910, the tree had already earned a place in Elwes and Henry's authoritative survey The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland, which singled it out as the finest specimen of its kind in the entire country, a claim about a tree that may have been, functionally, one of a kind to begin with. It has grown considerably since, from under 12 metres tall in 1910 to nearly 17 metres with a 19.5 metre crown spread by a 2005 measurement, though a butt-decaying fungus now regularly fruits on its trunk each autumn, a visible sign of age and decline rather than imminent death. The garden has already grafted a younger replacement, planted near the Terrace Garden in 1991, as insurance for whenever the original eventually goes.

trees.verify_notes: Garden page: Main Walk grouping of Black/Austrian Pine subspecies, 'large, mature trees date from the earliest plantings in the 1840s'; garden established 1846. Most extreme contrast is the pair ssp nigra (Austria, downward-sloping unbranched limbs, short stiff needles) opposite ssp salzmannii (Spain, immense upward-spreading branches, open canopy of long needles); nearby ssp pallasiana (Crimean) and ssp laricio (Corsican). Placed deliberately by John Stevens Henslow, Darwin's mentor, to show variation within a species; positioned in the high-profile spot where symmetry would be expected. cam.ac.uk news 8 May 2023: the black pine was lit by pedal-power in the Coronation concert on 7 May 2023, 'one of the first Garden plantings' (alive evidence, 2023; garden page current). Age derived from garden's 1840s planting statement for the group, not a per-tree date; no girth or height given anywhere. Both sources are the owner (garden and university): one owner, flagged. Pin is the garden's centroid (Wikipedia 52.19361, 0.12722), not the tree; garden is 16 ha, tree position within it not fixed from a source. One collectible point: the opposed pair, one place to stand. Garden's separate black-pine trail page exists (learning/trails/speciation/blackpine) but not fetched.
trees.story:
Darwin's teacher planted these pines so that they would look wrong. John Stevens Henslow, the botanist who mentored Charles Darwin at Cambridge, set out the Botanic Garden's Main Walk with black pines facing each other in pairs, exactly where a visitor expects symmetry, and then chose trees that refuse to match.

The starkest pair stands directly opposite one another. On one side is the Austrian form, with slender, unbranched limbs sloping downward and short, stiff needles. On the other is the Spanish form, its immense branches spreading upward into an open crown of long needles. Same species, different countries, and the difference is the lesson. Crimean and Corsican black pines stand nearby to make the point twice more.

The garden says its large black pines date from the earliest plantings of the 1840s, soon after it was established in 1846, which puts the pair at roughly 180 years. It gives no planting date for either tree on its own, and no girth or height has been published.

They are still part of the garden's life rather than its archive. On 7 May 2023, during the Coronation concert, one of the black pines was lit up by people pedalling bicycles to make the power. The garden is ticketed and about fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two black pines facing each other across the Main Walk, one with slender limbs sloping downward, the other with huge branches spreading upward into an open crown.

A 1915 survey by the curator records one original tree blown down in 1886; suckers were allowed to grow up afterwards (also Trees and Shrubs Online). trees.story:
In 1886 a storm brought down one of the two Caucasian wingnuts planted beside the stream that feeds the Botanic Garden's Lake. The gardeners did not clear the ground. They let the suckers come up, and what stands there now is an immense thicket of stems, the tallest of them as tall as the original tree.

That is why this entry is a stand rather than a single trunk. The suckers have been left to grow for well over a century, straddling the stream so that it is hard to say where one tree ends and the next begins. The garden counts it among its most outstanding features. The Tree Register measured the tallest stem at 27 metres in 2004, a figure quoted by Trees and Shrubs Online.

The record of the 1886 loss comes from a 1915 survey by the garden's curator. Nobody has published when the original pair went in. The garden was established in 1846 and the trees were standing before the storm, so they were planted somewhere in those forty years, which makes the stand at least 140 years old in its roots. The clone itself is the living continuation of those first two trees.

In late summer long green chains of winged nutlets hang from the branches. The garden is ticketed, fifteen minutes on foot from the station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a thicket of tall wingnut stems rather than a single trunk, straddling the stream that runs into the Lake.

best_time.label: late summer, when long green chains of winged nutlets hang from the branches

trees.story:
The Botanic Garden calls this the first dawn redwood to grow on British soil since the Mesozoic era, the age of the dinosaurs. Its seed was collected in China in 1946 and 1947 and sent by a Dr Silow to Professor F. T. Brooks in Cambridge. Two seedlings were planted out beside the Lake in 1949, according to that year's annual report.

The garden has kept a record of its growth ever since. It was 1.5 metres tall in 1952, 17 metres by 1977 and close to 23 metres in 2002, the last figure published. In that same year it was chosen as one of fifty Great British Trees to mark the Queen's Golden Jubilee.

That puts it at about 77 years old, young by the standards of this site but with a lineage most old trees cannot match. Emmanuel and Clare colleges also hold dawn redwoods from the same collection, by their own accounts, so the claim to be first is the garden's.

The tree stands on the south-western shore of the Lake, next to the garden's giant redwood, two very different trees with the same family name side by side. Unlike most conifers it drops its needles in winter. In late autumn they turn a foxy reddish brown before they fall. The garden is ticketed, fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in autumn by the needles turning reddish brown, and in winter by its bare branches, unlike the evergreen giant redwood. It stands beside that redwood on the south-western shore of the Lake.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn foxy reddish brown and fall

trees.story:
In 1915 the garden's curator, Richard Lynch, recorded this pine at 5.4 metres. It has since reached 14.4, and the Botanic Garden says no other specimen in the British Isles appears to have grown so well. In the language of tree recorders, that makes it a champion, the best example of its kind in the country.

This is a rarity entry rather than an ancient one. The Chilgoza pine, also called Gerard's pine, is not a tree most visitors will have met, and what earns this one its place is how well it has done in a Cambridge garden, nearly tripling its height since the First World War.

That 1915 measurement is the oldest fact on record about it, and it tells you the tree was already established then. When it was planted, the garden does not say, and no one has published an estimate of its age. If you know, tell us.

The champion status rests on the garden's own account rather than a published register entry, so read the crown as the garden's claim. It stands on the Main Walk, the same avenue as the paired black pines Henslow planted, and the garden is ticketed, about fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the Chilgoza pine on the Main Walk, 14.4 metres tall, the garden's champion of its kind. Look for the species label, since the pin marks the garden rather than the tree.

trees.story:
In 2000 a storm heaved this pine's roots out of the ground. It did not go over. It came to rest on one of its lower branches, and the Botanic Garden says it has continued to thrive from there.

The garden counts its single-leaf nut pine among the earliest tree plantings it has. At the start of the twentieth century it stood just under three metres. It was recorded recently at 11.8, enough to make it a champion tree, and the garden says it far exceeds many specimens growing in the wild.

The wild is a long way off. Pinus monophylla comes from the semi-desert of Nevada and California, and it is the only pine with single needles. The garden puts its success in Cambridge down to the city's dry climate.

It still produces large, viable seeds, the pinyon nuts that were a staple food for California's indigenous peoples before Columbus.

Nobody has published a planting date, so its exact age is open. If you know when it went in, tell us. Its champion status rests on the garden's own account, as the measurements do.

It grows in the Old Pinetum. A second single-leaf pine there, planted in 1965, has reached 6.3 metres, so the old tree is the taller by five and a half. The garden is ticketed, about fifteen minutes on foot from Cambridge station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the way it rests on one lower branch, where a storm in 2000 left it, 11.8 metres tall. It stands in the Old Pinetum, near a younger single-leaf pine of 6.3 metres.
